Homework 4: Optical Flow

Submission Instructions. Your submission should be a zip file, containing at least this Marimo notebook (just like previous weeks) as well as handwritten work attached as a PDF (hw4.pdf) for the written questions. Notation. As in the notes, ||(x||) runs to the right and ||(y||) runs down. ||((u,v)||) is the motion from frame ||(t||) to frame ||(t+1||) in pixels, with ||(u||) along ||(x||) and ||(v||) along ||(y||). ||(I_t = I (x,y,t+1) - I (x,y,t)||) is the frame difference. Over a window, Lucas–Kanade solves ||(\mathtt{A} \,\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{b}||) with: ||[ \mathtt{A} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{12} & a_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \left\langle I_x ^{2} \right\rangle & \left\langle I_x I_y \right\rangle \\ \left\langle I_x I_y \right\rangle & \left\langle I_y ^{2} \right\rangle \end{bmatrix}, ||]||[ \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \left\langle I_x I_t \right\rangle \\ \left\langle I_y I_t \right\rangle \end{bmatrix}, ||]||[ \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\det\mathtt{A} } \begin{bmatrix} -a_{22}\, b_1 + a_{12}\, b_2 \\ \phantom{-}a_{12}\, b_1 - a_{11}\, b_2 \end{bmatrix}, ||]where the angle brackets are sums over the window (here with ||(w = 1||)). The eigenvalues of ||(\mathtt{A}||) are: ||[ \lambda_{1,2} = \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}\mathtt{A} \pm \sqrt{(\tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}\mathtt{A})^2 - \det\mathtt{A}}, ||]with ||(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2||) (Lecture 3).
Problem 1: One pixel at a time

1(a)

Start from brightness constancy, ||[ I(x+u,\, y+v,\, t+1) = I(x,\, y,\, t), ||]and derive the optical flow constraint equation ||[ I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0, ||]with ||(I_t||) the frame difference. Say which step is an approximation, and when that approximation is good.

Your answer to Problem 1(a). Brightness constancy says a point keeps its brightness as it moves: I(x+u, y+v, t+1) = I(x, y, t) The unknowns u and v sit inside the image function, so we linearize with a first-order Taylor expansion. Starting from the brightness at (x, y) in frame t+1, we add the slope times the step in each direction, where I_x and I_y are the spatial derivatives of the image: I(x+u, y+v, t+1) ≈ I(x, y, t+1) + I_x u + I_y v Frame t+1 equals frame t plus the frame difference, I_t = I(x, y, t+1) − I(x, y, t). This is exact: I(x, y, t+1) = I(x, y, t) + I_t Substituting: I(x+u, y+v, t+1) ≈ I(x, y, t) + I_x u + I_y v + I_t By brightness constancy the left side equals I(x, y, t), so: I(x, y, t) ≈ I(x, y, t) + I_x u + I_y v + I_t The I(x, y, t) terms cancel, leaving the optical flow constraint equation: I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0 Which step is the approximation? Only the first-order Taylor expansion. Rewriting frame t+1 as frame t plus I_t is exact. When is it good? When the motion is small (about a pixel or less in a sharp image). For larger motions the brightness no longer varies linearly over the step, so the linear approximation breaks down.

In this problem you write Lucas–Kanade, test it on frames whose motion is known, and then use it on two frames of the drive from Lecture 5. Verify that you have the following five images in a directory data/hw4/.

board_t1_small.png frame ||(t+1||): the board moved by ||((u,v) = (0.6,\ 0.45)||) pixels

The board frames were made by moving the photograph by an exact amount, which need not be a whole number of pixels, and adding a small amount of noise to each frame. The true flow is therefore known at every pixel. Settings. Use the settings of the notes throughout. Blur each frame lightly with a Gaussian before taking derivatives (the notebook gives ||(\sigma||)). For ||(I_x||) and ||(I_y||), take central differences of frame ||(t||) divided by 2, as in the notes: ||[ I_x = \big(I(x{+}1, y) - I(x{-}1, y)\big)/2. ||]Use the frame difference for ||(I_t||) and a ||(7\times7||) window with ||(w = 1||). Intensities are in ||([0, 1]||). Positions are ||((x, y)||), with ||(x||) along a row and ||(y||) down, so pixel ||((x, y)||) is I[y, x]. (Homework 3 used (row, col).) Implement lk_point for the one-step estimate at a single point in part (a), grid_optical_flow for the grid of one-step estimates in part (b), and optical_flow for the iterative, pyramidal flow field in part (c). You may reuse your code from Homework 3 where useful. In optical_flow, follow Section 5.10: at each pyramid level, from the top down, sample frame ||(t+1||) at the window's pixels moved by the current estimate, form ||(I_t||) and ||(\mathbf{b}||), solve for the correction, and repeat. Going down one level, double the estimate. Implementation conventions. For a multichannel image in ||([0, 1]||), convert to grayscale with Image.fromarray((image * 255).astype(np.uint8)).convert("L"), then convert the result to floating point and divide by 255. For smoothing, use scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter(image, sigma, mode="reflect", truncate=4.0). You may ignore all boundary effects. Problem 5: Optical Flow for Tracking

One application of optical flow is for tracking points in video sequences. In this exercise, you will use your optical flow function to track keypoints in the video sequence displayed below. Start by extracting keypoint proposals. We'll use OpenCV's implementation of SIFT to do this using cv2.SIFT_create. Read the documentation for the function, then implement the extract_keypoints function below, which should return a numpy array of shape (N, 2), where N is the maximum number of keypoints retained. We provide the visualization code for the SIFT keypoints in the cells below.

Then, estimate the keypoint's new position ||((x_f, y_f) \approx (x_i + u, y_i + v)||). We will refer to these tracked keypoints at frame 1 as ||(P_1||) which also has a shape of ||((N, 2)||).
  3. Using the tracked keypoints at frame 1, ||(P_1||), compute the tracked keypoints at frame 2 ||(P_2||). Repeat this to compute ||(P_3, P_4, ..., P_{K - 1}||).
